newsitem.title: GREECE: Greeks pin hopes on Euro court for cheaper cars.
newsitem.headline: Greeks pin hopes on Euro court for cheaper cars.

text.p: Greek consumers have pinned their hopes of cheaper cars on a speedy court ruling against Athens, which has been accused by the European Commission of giving unequal tax treatment on new and used cars imported from EU countries.
The car taxation issue re-emerged after a Sunday newspaper report that the finance ministry favoured reducing an unpopular consumption tax on used cars from the EU.
The Sunday Eleftherotypia quoted Deputy Finance Minister George Drys as saying it was time to import cheap used cars which were less than three years old from other EU states.
The report enraged car importers who accused the government of being irresponsible and said this decision would freeze the car market for a few months and hurt car importing companies.
Drys appeared to reverse course on Monday, saying lower taxes on imported used cars from EU countries would not occur before the end of 1997 or 1998.

"In February, we will go to the European Court where the European Commission has taken us. It will take six to eight months for the final verdict. By the time the decision has been taken, 1997 will be gone," he told state radio ERA.
Greece levies extraordinary taxes on used cars with special consumption tax rates as high as 400 percent compared to 75 percent for new cars.
The European Commission took Greece to the European Court in 1995 for violating EU rules. Portugal has faced a similar case.

"We believe the European Court will rule against us but it is preferable to have a drawn out process for fiscal reasons," said a finance ministry official who requested anonymity. "This has been our strategy from the beginning and it has worked."
Greece is struggling to put its public finances in order to meet Maastricht single currency criteria. Car taxes are expected to reach 150 billion drachmas in 1996.

A European Court spokesman told Reuters that the written procedure on the case finished in April. The next stage is oral hearings but this is unlikely to happen before February because it is not in the present calendar which runs until mid-February.
It usually takes six to 10 weeks before the advocate general expresses an opinion and then it can take another two to three months before the final verdict.
Greece is arguing against reducing consumption taxes on used cars to bring them into line with existing ones on new cars citing environmental concerns.
But Greek consumers did not buy the arguments and praised the Commission for taking Greece to court.

"What has the state done for environmental problems in Athens or other cities?" asked Aris Fotopoulos, who works for a private company and wants to buy a used car. "They have suddenly become environmentalists over used cars because they are afraid they will collect less in taxes."
Fotopoulos praised the Commission for taking action against Greece and expressed hope the European court would move swiftly.
"I just hope the court issues a decision soon," he said.
